Targets: base class and ship¶

Every scattering target (the ocean, a ship) shares one small interface so the link budget can treat them the same way. This page covers the abstract base and the ship model; the ocean model has its own page (Ocean target).

Target base¶

Summary¶

Target is the abstract base for any RCS model. It defines one method, compute_rcs(geometry, wavelength_m, illuminated_area_m2), which returns a TargetRcs – the RCS per sample plus an info dictionary of diagnostics. The illuminated_area_m2 argument is for distributed (area-extensive) targets like the ocean; point targets such as a ship ignore it. This shared interface is what lets the link budget swap one target for another without changing.

Ship target¶

Summary¶

ShipTarget models a ship as a simple box of metal surfaces and returns its radar cross-section. The hull is broken into five flat plates (deck, port side, starboard side, bow, stern) and two hull-water dihedrals (the right-angle corner where each side meets the sea, which are strong retroreflectors). Each plate uses the flat-plate formula and each dihedral the corner formula from Cross-cutting helpers (rotations, functions, ship_physics). The pieces add up without phase (non-coherently), and the info dict keeps the per-piece breakdown. This is an ideal-conductor engineering surrogate for aspect studies, not a validated absolute ship-RCS model.

The ship body frame¶

Each sample builds a ship frame from the heading and the local up direction:

(68)¶\[\hat{b} = \text{heading (flattened onto the sea)}, \qquad \hat{m} = \hat{n}_\mathrm{surface}, \qquad \hat{s} = \hat{b} \times \hat{m},\]

i.e. bow \(\hat{b}\) (forward), mast \(\hat{m}\) (up), and starboard \(\hat{s}\) (right). The five plates and two dihedrals are placed in this frame, each evaluated with its own bistatic visibility, and summed:

(69)¶\[\sigma_\mathrm{ship} = \sum_{\text{5 plates}} \sigma_\mathrm{plate} + \sum_{\text{2 dihedrals}} \sigma_\mathrm{dihedral}.\]

compute_rcs(geometry, wavelength_m, illuminated_area_m2=None)[source]¶

Per-sample ship RCS as the non-coherent sum of five plates and two hull-water dihedrals.

illuminated_area_m2 is ignored: a ship is a point target with an absolute RCS. The info dict breaks the total down per plate and per dihedral.

Parameters:

  • geometry (BistaticGeometry)

  • wavelength_m (float)

  • illuminated_area_m2 (np.ndarray | None)

Return type:

TargetRcs

Module Assumptions and Limitations¶

  • Box geometry. The ship is a rectangular box (plates + waterline dihedrals); superstructure, masts, curved hulls, and material effects are not modelled.

  • Ideal PEC and scalar response. Plates are perfectly conducting and use a scalar physical-optics form factor. Polarisation matrices, diffraction, creeping waves and edge interactions are omitted.

  • Simplified dihedral. The dihedral uses an ideal peak with an along-edge sinc and binary open-wedge visibility. It omits the full angular/polarimetric response, finite leg diffraction and coupling to a rough moving sea.

  • Non-coherent sum. Components add in power, not amplitude, so interference between facets is not captured.

  • Above-waterline only. Only the freeboard (above-water) part contributes; the submerged hull does not return at L-band.

  • Deterministic, not stochastic. RCS is a fixed function of aspect; real ships fluctuate with roll, pitch, and yaw (a planned refinement).

  • No absolute calibration. Tests verify implementation identities and visibility rules only. They do not compare against full-wave simulation, an RCS database or measurements, so absolute received power and detection range should be treated as preliminary.

User Guide¶

The ship dimensions come from the [SHIP] section of the moving-target config:

Table 19: [SHIP] keys¶

Key

Meaning

Unit

length_m

Ship length.

m

Ship width.

When [SHIP] is set, the detector evaluates the ship return at each detection event; otherwise the run is ocean-only.
